metadata.title: The impact of ICT and robots on labour market outcomes of demographic groups in Europe

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: The study uses worker-level data from the EU Structure of Earnings Survey (EU-SES) merged with sector-level technology measures (ICT capital from Eurostat/EU-KLEMS and robot exposure from IFR) and then estimates within-sector demographic-group regressions. Instead of ILSA-style sampling weights, the authors apply “standardised weights (based on 2010 sectoral employment shares)” to give every country equal weight in the baseline estimation; they also implement an alternative weighting scheme using the square root of observed employees as a robustness check. The paper does not report any replicate-weight scheme (e.g., BRR/jackknife) and does not describe complex survey variance estimation; standard errors are clustered at the sector-year level. Because the analysis is econometric (OLS/2SLS with IV) rather than ML prediction, the concept of survey weights for representativeness is handled through these country-sector weighting choices rather than PV-based survey-weight procedures.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: This paper does not use plausible values (PVs) because the dependent variables are labour-market outcomes constructed from EU-SES (employment shares, relative hourly wages, and wage-bill shares) and the technology exposures are sector-level capital measures; PVs are not part of this econometric design. Missing-data handling is not described in the provided text beyond sample exclusions based on minimum observation counts for demographic-group/occupation cells, so the specific treatment of item-level or record-level missingness is not documented.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The study covers 14 European countries (Belgium, Czechia, Germany, Estonia, Greece, Spain, Finland, France, Italy, Lithuania, Latvia, the Netherlands, Norway, Sweden) for 2010–2018 where EU-SES, ICT (Eurostat/EU-KLEMS), robot (IFR), and OECD TiVA data are available. The baseline unit of analysis is a demographic group (gender × four age groups: 20–29, 30–49, 50–59, 60+) within a country–sector cell. For the baseline demographic-group regressions, the authors drop groups with fewer than 15 observations in any year; the remaining worker-level observations total 21.2 million. For occupation-type mechanism analyses, they re-estimate regressions separately for four occupation task groups (non-routine cognitive, routine cognitive, routine manual, non-routine manual) and drop outcome variables for cells with fewer than 10 observations.

main_findings.dataset_used: PIAAC (used only as background evidence; not the estimation dataset) — OECD adult problem-solving in technology-rich environments (age comparisons)
main_findings.target_variable: Age differences in technology-rich problem-solving performance (background)
main_findings.performance_metrics: Not reported (cited descriptive PIAAC evidence: ~50% of ages 25–34 vs 24% ages 45–54 vs 12% ages 55–65 at Level 2/3).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PIAAC background evidence, the study leverages age-related differences in problem-solving performance in technology-rich environments to contextualize heterogeneous labour-market responses to ICT and robots, finding that younger adults are substantially more likely to be at higher proficiency levels. This indicates that lifelong learning and skill-upgrading policies for older workers may be necessary to mitigate technology-driven labour-market disadvantages, though the paper’s main causal estimates are not derived from PIAAC.

main_findings.dataset_used: EU-SES (2010–2018) merged with Eurostat/EU-KLEMS ICT capital and IFR robot exposure — within-sector demographic groups (gender × age) outcomes
main_findings.target_variable: Employment share change (percentage points) — women age 20–29
main_findings.performance_metrics: 2SLS (Table 3A): Δ ICT capital coefficient 0.129 (p<0.1; SE 0.066); Δ Robots coefficient 0.201 (p<0.01; SE 0.060). Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F: 33.7; N=558 (women 20–29).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using EU-SES (2010–2018) data merged with sector ICT capital and robot exposure, the study leveraged ICT capital exposure and robot exposure (with controls for GVC participation, lagged tertiary education share, and country-year fixed effects) to predict four-year changes in women’s employment shares by age group within sectors, finding that higher ICT capital and higher robot exposure both increased the employment share of women aged 20–29 in 2SLS estimates. This indicates that technology adoption can expand employment opportunities for younger women, suggesting that labour-market policies should support entry pathways and job-matching for demographic groups that benefit from ICT/automation-driven demand.

main_findings.dataset_used: EU-SES (2010–2018) merged with Eurostat/EU-KLEMS ICT capital and IFR robot exposure — within-sector demographic groups (gender × age) outcomes
main_findings.target_variable: Employment share change (percentage points) — women age 60+
main_findings.performance_metrics: 2SLS (Table 3D): Δ ICT capital coefficient -0.105 (p<0.01; SE 0.041); Δ Robots coefficient -0.125 (p<0.01; SE 0.039). Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F: 29.0; N=496 (women 60+).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using EU-SES (2010–2018) data merged with sector ICT capital and robot exposure, the study leveraged ICT capital exposure and robot exposure (with controls for GVC participation, lagged tertiary education share, and country-year fixed effects) to predict four-year changes in women’s employment shares by age group within sectors, finding that both higher ICT capital and higher robot exposure reduced the employment share of women aged 60+ in 2SLS estimates. This indicates that older women may be left behind by routine-replacing technologies, supporting policy priorities such as targeted reskilling, mobility support, and incentives for firms to retain and redeploy older workers.

main_findings.dataset_used: EU-SES (2010–2018) merged with Eurostat/EU-KLEMS ICT capital and IFR robot exposure — within-sector demographic groups (gender × age) outcomes
main_findings.target_variable: Employment share change (percentage points) — men age 30–49
main_findings.performance_metrics: 2SLS (Table 3B): Δ ICT capital coefficient 0.156 (p<0.05; SE 0.066); Δ Robots coefficient -0.202 (p<0.05; SE 0.091). Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F: 37.4; N=596 (men 30–49).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using EU-SES (2010–2018) data merged with sector ICT capital and robot exposure, the study leveraged ICT capital exposure and robot exposure (with controls for GVC participation, lagged tertiary education share, and country-year fixed effects) to predict four-year changes in men’s employment shares by age group within sectors, finding that ICT capital increased employment shares for men aged 30–49 while robot exposure decreased them in 2SLS estimates. This indicates that automation may disproportionately displace prime-aged men in routine tasks, so policy should combine technology transition support with targeted employment protection and training for affected occupational segments.

main_findings.dataset_used: EU-SES (2010–2018) merged with Eurostat/EU-KLEMS ICT capital and IFR robot exposure — within-sector demographic groups (gender × age) outcomes
main_findings.target_variable: Employment share change (percentage points) — men age 50–59
main_findings.performance_metrics: 2SLS (Table 3C): Δ ICT capital coefficient -0.022 (not significant; SE 0.033); Δ Robots coefficient 0.109 (p<0.05; SE 0.054). Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F: 46.6; N=592 (men 50–59).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using EU-SES (2010–2018) data merged with sector ICT capital and robot exposure, the study leveraged ICT capital exposure and robot exposure (with controls for GVC participation, lagged tertiary education share, and country-year fixed effects) to predict four-year changes in men’s employment shares by age group within sectors, finding that robot exposure increased the employment share of men aged 50–59 while ICT capital showed no statistically significant effect in 2SLS estimates. This indicates that older prime men may benefit from automation-driven restructuring in some contexts, implying that employment policies should be age-sensitive and occupationally targeted rather than assuming uniform displacement.

main_findings.dataset_used: EU-SES (2010–2018) merged with Eurostat/EU-KLEMS ICT capital and IFR robot exposure — within-sector demographic groups (gender × age) outcomes
main_findings.target_variable: Relative wage change (percentage of sector average) — women age 20–29
main_findings.performance_metrics: 2SLS (Table 4A): Δ ICT capital coefficient 0.001 (SE 0.123); Δ Robots coefficient 0.049 (SE 0.211); no statistically significant IV effects reported. Kleibergen-Paap rk Wald F: 33.7; N=558 (women 20–29).
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using EU-SES (2010–2018) data merged with sector ICT capital and robot exposure, the study leveraged ICT capital exposure and robot exposure (with controls for GVC participation, lagged tertiary education share, and country-year fixed effects) to predict four-year changes in women’s relative wages within sectors, finding that IV (2SLS) effects on relative wages were not statistically significant for women aged 20–29. This indicates that technology adoption may primarily reallocate employment across groups rather than systematically changing relative pay, suggesting wage-focused interventions alone may be insufficient without employment and matching policies.

data.outcome_summary: This paper studies how ICT and industrial robots affect labour-market outcomes of demographic groups in Europe using EU-SES worker-level data merged with sector-level technology measures from Eurostat/EU-KLEMS (ICT capital) and the International Federation of Robotics (IFR) (robot exposure), covering 14 countries over 2010–2018. The authors estimate within-sector demographic-group models for employment shares, relative hourly wages, and wage-bill shares, using OLS and two-stage least squares (2SLS) with an instrumental-variable strategy that instruments technology growth using “technology frontier” growth in the United States. In 2SLS results (e.g., Table 3), ICT capital increases employment shares for young and prime-aged women but reduces employment shares for women aged 60+, while robot exposure reduces employment shares for young/prime-aged men in routine manual contexts and can increase employment shares for some older men. Relative wages show barely any statistically significant IV effects (Table 4), implying employment reallocation dominates wage effects. The study applies country-sector weighting based on 2010 sectoral employment shares (and alternative weights in robustness checks) and clusters standard errors at the sector-year level; it does not use PVs, and missing-data handling for micro records is not explicitly documented in the provided text.
